items.title: 5 BI staffers who put AI agents to work share what worked and what went wrong
items.summary: Rebecca Zisser/BI 5 BI staffers told us how they've been using the hottest new thing in AI: personal AI agents. Their use cases include reserving library books and collecting K-pop merch. One editor used it to remind him to call his mother. Muse and Instinct — AI agents designed to help you run your personal life — are the talk of the town right now. So, obviously, we at Business Insider had to try them out. Five staffers across the newsroom's global offices — from headquarters in New York to divisions in London, San Francisco, and Singapore — have been testing both Meta and Instinct's personal AI agent offerings over the past week. Our editor-in-chief, Jamie Heller, got in on the action, too: My husband and I were puzzling over an opaquely described charge on our credit card. We put the wording into Chat GPT and Muse — asking each what it could be. Chat couldn't figure it out. Muse did.
items.summary_html:
Rebecca Zisser/BI

  • 5 BI staffers told us how they've been using the hottest new thing in AI: personal AI agents.
  • Their use cases include reserving library books and collecting K-pop merch.
  • One editor used it to remind him to call his mother.

Muse and Instinct — AI agents designed to help you run your personal life — are the talk of the town right now.

So, obviously, we at Business Insider had to try them out. Five staffers across the newsroom's global offices — from headquarters in New York to divisions in London, San Francisco, and Singapore — have been testing both Meta and Instinct's personal AI agent offerings over the past week.

Our editor-in-chief, Jamie Heller, got in on the action, too:

My husband and I were puzzling over an opaquely described charge on our credit card. We put the wording into Chat GPT and Muse — asking each what it could be. Chat couldn't figure it out. Muse did.

Keep reading for our 101 on what worked, and what didn't. And if you have an experience of your own to share, fill out our survey.

In response to our requests for comment, a Meta spokesperson pointed us to a dedicated safety post on its website. Instinct did not respond to our request for comment.

Will Martin, senior editor, used Instinct to pay a car fee, but it backfired

Will Martin

I downloaded Instinct two weeks ago and chose a very simple task to start with: Remind me to call my mother (she worries).

My whoa moment: Instinct jumped to my aid when I told it I needed a new torque wrench for my bike. After a simple prompt, Instinct came back with four options: a cheap one, a mid-priced option, and two higher-end versions — all with links and a pro/con list.

In the two weeks I've been using it, Instinct has created an itinerary for a weekend trip I'm taking next year, booked tickets for my daily commute into London, and secured me a refund on an $80 subscription I forgot to cancel after the free trial.

My yikes moment: This past weekend, I took a trip to Oxford, one of Britain's most notoriously complex places to drive. Oxford is famed as a warren of one-way streets, traffic cameras, and tolls.

I asked my Instinct agent to pay the city's congestion charge after I drove in. Instinct obliged, cross-checking my car's model against the different emissions tiers for the charging zone, and sending me a confirmation that it had paid for two days at £4 per day.

As I touted how easy it all was to my AI-skeptical partner, she pointed out that the cost was £5, not £4. So I checked, and it turned out Instinct got it wrong — it had paid a similar but separate charge for a smaller area of the city. The charge was nonrefundable, so I was forced to swallow both my own pride and an £8 tax for trusting the robots. Lesson learned, even if Instinct tried to find a silver lining.

Cheryl Teh, senior news editor, used Instinct to expand her K-pop merch collection
Cheryl used Instinct to formulate a targeted plan to buy K-pop albums

Cheryl Teh

Some people use their AI agents to save money. I decided to do the opposite and ask it to tell me how to spend my money.

My whoa moment: I'm a K-pop fan, and my favorite stars — Jeonghan and Joshua, from the group Seventeen — opened preorders for their new album "Dreamscape" on Wednesday morning.

I didn't have the time or energy to parse through all the listings for "preorder bonus" gifts; things like limited-run photocards and polaroids that go to fans who place their orders early. Collecting limited edition K-pop merchandise can be a bit of a blood sport, so I wanted a solid strategy.

I asked Instinct to create a "buy plan" to maximize my fan experience. It took three minutes to surface a link to exclusive signed copies available for early orders on the band's US website. The agent also gave me a road map for purchase quantities and the optimal time to make those orders.

Instinct saved me two hours with one prompt. Without it, I would have missed the window to purchase the US-only autographed albums.

I did receive a bit of judgment from the agent — it asked me not once but twice if I'd set a cut-off budget for my buy plan. I had not, and did not intend to set one!

I haven't plucked up the courage to give the agent my credit card details yet, though.

My yikes moment: I was less impressed during my first 24 hours of using Instinct, when I added it to my Notion dashboard and asked it to do an overhaul. It ended up clearing out my goals calendar and schedule, and replacing it with a new — but blank — template.

Instinct's WhatsApp-based chat feature is intuitive and consumer-friendly. But for optimal results, you've got to be precise in your prompts, and lay out exactly and unambiguously what you want the agent to do.

Tim Paradis, future of work correspondent, put Instinct to work booking a movie ticket
Instinct was helpful with some things, but also gave incorrect information.

Tim Paradis

The other day, I asked Instinct whether tickets were available for a 6:30 p.m. showing of "Spider-Man: Brand New Day" at a nearby theater.

My whoa moment: We were on our way when Instinct texted that there wasn't a 6:30. It was 6:15, "which starts in about 8 minutes." Thank goodness for trailers — and for a speedy driver (which wasn't me). Instinct said online sales had ended, so "your only shot" was the box office. It also started checking backup films.

My yikes moment: It suggested a 6:50 "Spider-Man" at another theater, but said tickets "were glitching," and gave me the theater's number. Obviously, because no one died, I wasn't going to call. The theater's site showed no "Spider-Man" that night. I told Instinct, and 16 minutes later, it said the movie "likely got pulled back." By then, we had our tickets at the original theater. "Enjoy the movie!" Instinct said.

Katie Notopoulos, senior correspondent, used Muse to sign an after-school care form

Katie Notopoulos

My whoa moment: Most of the tasks I wanted it to do for me were related to the morass of messages and paperwork from my kids' school and activities. However, it got stuck on things like logging into the clunky school site app or being unable to check out on the Girl Scouts website. But finally, a breakthrough — I had put off the task of printing out and signing a form for after-school care. I asked Muse to fill it out for me from my email. I sent it a photo of my signature on a Post-It and used a photo of my daughter's handwritten name (she was also supposed to sign it) as her signature (morally questionable, sure). It successfully "signed" it and emailed it back to the school.

My yikes moment: It offered to RSVP "no" to an invite in my email that happened to be on the same day as the Meta Connect conference. It suggested I could reply to the person and explain that this was "the most important event on my beat" — not totally wrong per se, but certainly weird to say in an email, and quite flattering to Meta.

Pranav Dixit, Meta correspondent, used Muse to place library holds

My whoa moment: I had one simple dream: outsource the stupidly fiddly work of finding books and placing library holds to an AI. I mapped Muse to my iPhone’s Action button and wired everything up by granting Muse access to my Libby account and my accounts at my two local libraries.

Now, when I ask Muse to look for a book, it checks Libby for a digital version and sends it to my Kindle if it's available immediately. If not, it compares the wait times on Libby and at my libraries, then places a hold on the copy that will get to me faster. Pressing one button to delegate a small slice of library bureaucracy feels slightly godlike.

My yikes moment: Amazon has blocked Muse, so I discovered that I can't connect it to Goodreads, the place that I keep track of all the books I want to read, and which Amazon owns. It was a reminder that a personal agent is only as useful as the platforms that allow it in. The minute this stuff becomes genuinely convenient, somebody puts up an anti-bot wall.

items.title: Five More Cops Charged for Abusing Flock Cameras Amid So Many Similar Scandals That We Can’t Even Keep Track
items.summary: Police abuse of AI-integrated surveillance cameras is spiraling out of control. On Wednesday, freshly unsealed court documents revealed that five Indianapolis police officers had been charged with abusing the department’s automatic license plate readers (ALPRs). The accused include officer Jonathan Schultz, an 18-year veteran, who used 300 cameras provided by the ALPR company Flock to stalk multiple women, including his ex-wife, and a woman he met at a workout class in 2023, ABC News reported . Ten hours away in North Carolina, the Franklin County Sheriff’s Office halted its Flock partnership and fired a seasoned detective who was caught using the cameras to “track the every movement of a single private citizen.” Across the country in San Jose, California, city officials are calling for a crackdown on police access to ALPRs after an officer was sacked for sharing Flock data with his cousin , who had been accused of domestic violence. Those are just the latest incidents involving police abuse of ALPRs, and are almost certain to be superseded by new scandals in the coming days and weeks. As Flock’s surveillance network swells to well over 140,000 ALPRs across the US, incidents of police abuse have followed, with at least 244 separate cases of police abuse recorded by the Institute for Justice — and those are just the ones who’ve gotten caught. Far from a few bad apples, the rate and distribution of ALPR abuse across the country points to a truly systemic issue, and one which isn’t stopping. The laundry list of ways police have abused Flock is immense — officers have been caught using ALPRs to stalk romantic interests , retaliate against critics , conduct unauthorized searches on behalf of immigration agents , monitor activists , harass coworkers , locate the victim of domestic abuse on behalf of the suspected perpetrator, surveil Muslims driving to mosques, and even just to pass the time when they’re bored. “Unfortunately, we have seen abuse of automated license plate readers for almost as long as they have existed,” senior investigative researcher for the Electronic Frontier Foundation Beryl Lipton said in an interview , after 10 officers from the Chicago area were caught abusing ALPRs in separate occasions in late August. “Previously, the systems weren’t as connected as they are,” Lipton said of Flocks expansive web of interconnected cameras. “Now that abuse can really take place at scale across state lines.” With so many angry protestors directing their rage at the company supplying these devices, it’s worth remembering who’s responsible for Flock’s real-world harms: unscrupulous police officers who treat innocent citizens like game to be tracked. More on Flock: Flock’s Network Is Losing Value to Cops as More and More of Its Cameras Go Offline

items.title: AI is prompting these Gen Zers to learn how to type
items.summary: Tom Vaughan-Mountford/Getty Images Gen Z grew up with phones and tablet typing, with many never learning keyboard skills. But in the age of AI-driven efficiency — and prompting — keyboard skills have a new use case. Some Gen Zers are becoming self-taught to avoid dictating AI prompts out loud. When Julia Andrusiak was in college, she noticed one of her professors repeatedly pausing his lecture. Eventually, she realized that she was the disruption: Her slow, two-finger typing was so loud that he couldn't concentrate. "It was the first moment I realized that I may not be the best at this," Andrusiak said. So she began drilling: First, she typed out books. That made her faster, but she was still staring at her keyboard. Then, she advanced to touch typing — typing without looking at the keyboard. She's still working on her speed and accuracy. Now 26, Andrusiak has an AI-focused job that involves helping people use the technology and sometimes necessitates writing strong prompts. She still can't type fast, so when she has a longer prompt, she dictates it — and feels self-conscious about what looks like talking to herself in an open office. In 2024, The Wall Street Journal reported that digital natives were baffling "teachers and parents with their lack of typing skills." Now, for some younger workers and students, typing is making a comeback . While AI might seem to harken a turn away from typing — who needs note-taking when you have an agent? — AI is only as good as the prompt it's given. Rambling voice prompts can be insufficiently clear and precise. The rise of AI has some Gen Zers looking for any efficiency edge they can carve out. "With the ever increasingly fast world, we need to type quicker. But I feel like people are really relying on AI," Andrusiak, who happily uses AI as an aid for writing and research, said. "One of my friends said, 'Well, you don't really have to type the whole page. You can just give it short sentences. It's not really that tiring.' But then I feel like it's outsourcing too much of cognitive power to a technology." Julia Andrusiak and her mechanical keyboard. Courtesy of Julia Andrusiak Typing as meditation and efficiency generator Andrey Gerasimov, a 23-year-old computer science graduate , never took typing classes. But he first needed the skill for his video game chats and decided to beef it up, eventually reaching 170 words per minute. As an AI user, he believes that faster typing makes for more efficient prompting. "You're going to be a lot more comfortable actually giving your full thoughts and ideas if you know that, hey, doing this is only going to take a minute," Gerasimov said. He's not the only one trying to up his speed and technique. In his decade teaching typing to 15 to 30-year-olds, Andreas Francazi, a 36-year-old IT teacher in Vienna, noticed that his students' typing skills have deteriorated — but they're setting out to change that. His newer crop of students didn't grow up around physical computers, and their familiarity with keyboards is much lower than previous typists. He's seen younger students come in typing rapidly with just two fingers, so he's teaching them the basics. Francazi said that students of all ages become entranced by a three-minute typing test, falling into a rapt silence. "The practice can be quite meditative," Francazi said. "You just sit there, you have the text in front of you, and you type character by character, and it kind of calms you a bit." While Francazi's screen-first students have mastered the art of two-finger typing, their future schooling and careers might necessitate the manual keyboarding skills he's teaching. Nick Sjolinder, the founder of BYOK — a purposefully distraction-free, digital typewriter device that connects to keyboards — said that around 10% of the device's orders are coming from educators, including elementary schools, middle schools, high schools, homeschools, and universities. A recent batch order came from a high school creative writing teacher, he said, with the intention of cutting down on AI and distractions for students. Tarun Krishnamurthy, an 18-year-old sophomore at San Diego State University, said his college professors speak quickly and tend to power through their slideshows. Krishnamurthi, who began intentionally practicing typing in middle school for fun, has an edge in keeping up. "I'm fortunate at least I can keep up with some of the professors, but I know some other students might have difficulty with that because they need to look at their keyboard instead of looking at the professor's slideshow," he said. And beyond fast classroom notetaking, Krishnamurthi sees his keyboard skills as a potential professional edge: In an ever-optimized and efficiency-focused world, "typing could be a big bottleneck." Slow typing could worsen workers' outputs, he said; his touch typing might give him an edge in an AI-ified world. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: The startup trap that kept this longevity app founder stuck
items.summary: Brent Franson is the CEO of Death Clock. Courtesy of Death Clock Death Clock CEO Brent Franson said startups can get stuck in a phase he calls "slow failure." He shut down his startup and threw out years' worth of code to build Death Clock, a consumer-health product. When a startup isn't viable , Franson says, founders should fully pivot rather than try to patch it. Brent Franson spent four years building a mental-health app that users liked, but that didn't ultimately work as a business. The product wasn't an obvious flop. It had enough promise, he said, to make further rounds of changes seem worthwhile — the trap of something that seemed "pretty good," though ultimately isn't viable. "Mediocrity is so dangerous," Franson said. In late 2024, seeing a need for a fresh start, he shut down the app, called Most Days, and discarded the codebase that his team had spent years building. The San Francisco-based staff then shifted their attention to building a consumer-health product called Death Clock, which Franson, 44, described as an "AI private doctor." Users enter health information — ranging from cholesterol levels to diet and sleep habits — and the platform uses longevity research to estimate the age at which they might die and suggest changes that could help them live longer. The experience reshaped how the longtime early-stage entrepreneur, who in 2019 sold a prior software company he ran to WeWork, thinks about startups. Here are three lessons Franson has learned: An app people like is not necessarily a viable business Most Days had users, though the company could not acquire them cheaply enough to build a sound business, he said. The scary part of pivoting , Franson said, is not when a business is clearly failing or obviously taking off. The product wasn't an obvious flop. It had enough promise, he said, to make further rounds of changes seem worthwhile — the trap of something that seemed "pretty good," though ultimately isn't viable.

"Mediocrity is so dangerous," Franson said.

In late 2024, seeing a need for a fresh start, he shut down the app, called Most Days, and discarded the codebase that his team had spent years building.

The San Francisco-based staff then shifted their attention to building a consumer-health product called Death Clock, which Franson, 44, described as an "AI private doctor."

Users enter health information — ranging from cholesterol levels to diet and sleep habits — and the platform uses longevity research to estimate the age at which they might die and suggest changes that could help them live longer.

An app people like is not necessarily a viable business

Most Days had users, though the company could not acquire them cheaply enough to build a sound business, he said.

The scary part of pivoting, Franson said, is not when a business is clearly failing or obviously taking off. It is when a product has users who like it and just enough promise to make another round of changes seem worthwhile.

"You can convince yourself to keep iterating on it," he said.

Franson, who is CEO of Death Clock, calls that danger "slow failure": a business that lingers because its leaders keep rationalizing why it might soon work. One test, he said, is whether founders are working through concrete problems with conviction or trying to talk themselves into continuing.

When you pivot, make a clean break

For Franson, the response wasn't to rebrand Most Days or look for another half-measure like a savvy hire. It was to shut it down completely.

He said the hardest decision was abandoning a company the team had spent years building and still believed served an important mental-health need. Yet, Franson said, the team concluded that they needed to make a clean break and a full bet on Death Clock.

The team carried no code from Most Days over to their new venture, Franson said.

The decision also meant embracing a name he initially saw as a potentially terrible mistake. The team had considered calling the product "More Years," Franson said, before deciding to keep the more provocative working name they had been using internally.

A good product needs a way to reach customers

Franson said the failure of Most Days taught him that product quality alone wouldn't cut it. A consumer company also needed a way to get attention without spending heavily to buy it, he said.

When Franson went to Most Days' investors about the shift, he said they faced a choice: Take back a fraction of their investment or support the Death Clock idea. Their reactions to the name were sharply divided, Franson said.

"People either loved the name Death Clock, or they hated it, but they didn't forget it," he said.

Death Clock's name comes with risks, he said, including whether the attention-grabbing approach will keep people from taking it seriously as a consumer-health product.

items.title: This small town librarian offers a 'Bye, Bye AI' class to take AI off your phone. Now everyone wants in.
items.summary: Shea Wert, library director of the North Chatham Free Library, will be holding a "Bye Bye AI" event to help people turn off AI features on their phones. Shea Wert A small upstate New York library is offering a "Bye Bye AI" event. The librarian will help people turn off AI features on their phones or email. She told BI she's also happy to help people set up AI. The event has gone viral, with people around the world wanting to tune in. North Chatham, a hamlet in upstate New York halfway between Hudson and Albany, doesn't have much going on. You have to go to the next hamlet over for a store or restaurant. There's a church, a post office, and a small public library with only about 800 cardholders. The North Chatham Free Library has gotten a lot of attention lately, however, after a flyer for an upcoming "Bye Bye AI" event offering to remove the AI features from your phone or laptop went viral on Facebook, getting over 200 comments and 8,000 likes. The poster was made by the library's sole full-time librarian, Shea Wert. Wert told Business Insider that she had made this event in response to community demand — and was surprised by the reaction from far-flung places. "Do I live anywhere near this library? No. Am I in support of this? Hell yeah!" wrote one commenter. The event flyer went viral on Facebook, getting comments from around the world. https://www.facebook.com/share/p/1J7QUQUcU2/ "I had to look at the library's main page to see where Chatham is. I'm in central CA and wonder if we can have a digital guide that our own Mariposa County Library could use for a similar program?" wrote another. "As someone in Ohio who just happened upon this post; will this be streamed or recorded?" someone else asked. "As somewhere near Chatham, UK, I was a little confused at first Regardless, thanks Shea!" a jolly Brit wrote. The library does weekly tech support drop-in hours, and in April it held an "AI for seniors" class that covered the basics of AI and LLMs. But this latest offering was something new. The idea was based on requests Wert had noticed from the community. "There's just been enough patrons asking about certain things that bothered them, specifically Gmail auto replies and auto completes really frustrate people," Wert told Business Insider during a recent phone call. "I went to a presentation that another librarian was doing about this topic, and they had had success with it. And I was like, 'Okay, well, I've heard enough from my patrons that they're worried about this stuff or frustrated about this stuff that I might as well try to do one.'" The library held an "AI for seniors" class earlier this year that covered the basics. North Chatham Free Library That other librarian, Hannah Cyrus, published a column in a journal of library studies, writing that "libraries have a role to play in facilitating patrons' rejection of technology, just as much as in their adoption of it." Cyrus has offered a series of free classes for patrons, teaching them how to turn off or avoid AI tools on their phones and computers, with great success — and a much larger turnout than other tech classes. TechCrunch reported in July that Cyrus's article in the library journal inspired other librarians to reach out and ask for help running their own versions of the classes. "I've heard from hundreds of librarians from all over the world asking for my presentation slides," she told Business Insider. The North Chatham Free Library serves a tiny hamlet in upstate New York, with only about 800 library card holders. Shea Wert One of the groups that reached out was a consortium of libraries for the Hudson Valley area, which included the North Chatham Free Library. Cyrus gave a webinar to a group of librarians, including Wert, about how she ran the "Avoiding AI" class. In Wert's personal life, she admits to staying a bit of a Luddite, preferring to use a dumbphone . But she's not adamantly anti-AI and has used AI tools for work to draft outlines or write dense policy text. "There have been some patrons that I know are using LLMs, and I'm happy to help them with it. I've helped them write better prompts, although that is far less common," she said. "It's more common that they haven't used it and they don't want to use it." Both Wert and Cyrus said that most of the people who come in for help with AI or tech in general are older adults, who are often frustrated by new AI features on the services they already use. The Bye-Bye AI event will take place next week, and Wert isn't entirely sure what to expect given the viral reaction on Facebook. "I'm a little concerned based on setting it up as a drop-in thing that there'll be people waiting because I can only help so many at one time," she said. "But I don't know. If 20 people come, that would feel like a lot to me." Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: David Rubenstein shares his recipe for career success — and says boomers like him 'don't want to get off the stage'
items.summary: David Rubenstein is the billionaire cofounder of Carlyle. Bloomberg/Getty Images David Rubenstein says reading, writing, speaking, and passion will serve young people in the AI era. The billionaire told Business Insider he swore off gambling at age 16 and won't retire anytime soon. The Baltimore Orioles owner just released a book featuring his interviews with other team owners. AI may be transforming the world of work , but the core ingredients for a successful career haven't changed, David Rubenstein says. "For a young person, the best thing to do is: Learn how to read and enjoy reading, learn how to speak effectively and persuasively , and learn how to write reasonably well," the billionaire investor told Business Insider in a recent, wide-ranging interview. The cofounder of private equity giant Carlyle also said to "find something that you really enjoy and make it your life's work." "If you really enjoy something, it's not work, and you'll do much better at it ," he continued. "Nobody ever won a Nobel Prize hating what they do." Rubenstein, 77, acknowledged that more and more people are relying on AI chatbots to read and write, but he said the ability to discern between good and bad writing will remain important. "I just think the basic skills that have gotten people to be successful over the last several thousand years are probably not going to go away ," he said. Rubenstein spoke to BI ahead of the release of his latest book this week: "Inside the Owner's Box: Conversations on Power and Leadership in Sports." Recipe for success The principal owner of the Baltimore Orioles baseball team also shared insights from his personal life. Rubenstein said that as a wealthy parent, he kept his children grounded by emphasizing the value of education and work ethic to them, and "tried to be a role model by showing how hard work can lead to something productive." All three of his kids went on to secure MBAs from Harvard or Stanford, and now work in private equity, he said. But he underscored that regardless of parents' best efforts, there's no guarantee how their children will turn out. Asked about work-life balance, Rubenstein said he doesn't view his work as a "chore" or "drudgery," and feels " fortunate that I can do things I really want to do." In recent years, he's pivoted from investing to interviewing everyone from Warren Buffett and Jamie Dimon to Bill and Hillary Clinton, while also publishing seven books and counting. Rubenstein said that owning a sports team has improved his work-life balance "because you have to go to games if you're going to be an effective owner , and I didn't go to that many games before." The Wall Street veteran also touched on sports betting, saying that after he lost $18 on a bet in high school, he swore off gambling for life. "I learned my lesson when I was 16," he said. Rubenstein said that if sports betting were to go away, "it wouldn't upset me, but I think it's here to stay." He also discussed the trend of baby boomers working later in life. He and a lot of his friends are working as hard in their mid-70s as they were 10 or 20 years earlier, he said, as "we don't want to get off the stage ." Rubenstein said he doesn't know what he'd do with himself if he retired, and he worries there's a greater risk of dropping dead after retirement. "So I'm not retiring anytime soon ," he said. items.title: Couples are using a viral AI agent to do their emotional labor. It’s been helpful — and chaotic.
items.summary: Some early adopters of Instinct are using AI agents to manage common tasks in a relationship, like shared to-do lists and vacation itineraries. It's had mixed results. Getty Images; BI Instinct's new "Trusted Person" allows users to connect their AI agents and tag-team tasks. Some couples use it for shared to-dos or help planning surprise date nights. While it cuts down on emotional labor, a therapist says not so fast: You still have to put work in. AI agents aren't just sneaking into your workplace anymore. Soon, they might be making regular appearances in your relationship. Since the launch of Instinct, an invite-only AI assistant that went viral among Silicon Valley insiders in August, early adopters have been using it to offload tasks like booking hotels and scheduling appointments. Then, on September 9, Noah Shinn, the company's 23-year-old founder, announced Instinct's new "Trusted Person" feature: You could now have your Instinct agent directly communicate with another person's Instinct agent to reduce the amount of "back-and-forth" in a relationship , such as coordinating plans and organizing vacations. Introducing our Trusted Person network powered by our new Instinct-to-Instinct communication protocol. Your Instinct can now talk to other Instincts to coordinate plans on your behalf. Getting people together often involves a lot of back-and-forth: finding a time, working out… pic.twitter.com/LXkDpXGmea — Noah Shinn (@noahrshinn) September 9, 2026 So far, some users have found it helpful. "Instinct syncs with my wife's Instinct so we can actually finish a shared to-do list," Alex Borkin, a 36-year-old entrepreneur who uses AI across his portfolio of companies, said on X , noting that it was easier than manually setting up AI agents using Claude Code or Codex. Have you used Instinct's "Trusted Person" feature with a spouse or partner? If you'd like to share your story, please reach out to jpugachevsky@businessinsider.com. While Instinct may help eradicate the most annoying part of a partnership (figuring out dinner plans when you both keep saying "whatever you want!"), it can also open up the possibilities of new relationship drama. Some users have already reported some issues, ranging from privacy concerns to accidentally spoiled surprises. Your emotional labor robot Emotional labor is disproportionately felt by women in relationships, causing friction. AI agents are marketed as reducing some of those responsibilities. janiecbros/Getty Images The greatest appeal of Instinct and other AI agents is their ability to cut down on what Borkin calls "boring tasks" — like booking appointments or getting refunds. "I close the loop," Borkin told Business Insider. "I get to go to bed and not think of 'Did I take care of jury duty?'" Like other working parents , Borkin and his wife use Instinct's Trusted Person feature to smooth out their day-to-day life as a family with two kids, ages 3 and 20 months (and a third child on the way). Most recently, the couple used Instinct agents to send them individual reminders to complete tasks for their daughter's third birthday party, such as ordering food. "It's nice not having to remind myself of something I asked my wife to help with, and then remind her if she's taking care of it," Borkin said. The more invisible work within a relationship — such as nudging a spouse to finish a task you asked them to do — requires cognitive and emotional labor . Some partners, more often women, can feel as though they bear the brunt of this work, leading to tension in the relationship. Annie Wright, a licensed psychotherapist who works with Silicon Valley clientele , told Business Insider that this dynamic is so common in heterosexual relationships that, sometimes, even AI agents don't fully solve the problem. "Even when you have an AI agent, who's putting in the prompt to begin with, who's architecting out the idea, who's remaining responsible for the oversight of that agent?" Wright said. More often than not, she said it's her female clients who are tasked with the burden. Wright said it can also be tempting to use AI agents as a way to avoid enduring "weaponized incompetence" when a partner performs the task wrong — or just keeps ignoring you. "An AI agent isn't going to bring that same relational scar tissue into the dynamic with you," she said. "It's very compelling. It provides a kind of shortcut, but it doesn't eliminate all the work for you." Deep intimacy required To book flights or fulfill shopping requests, AI agents need access to your credit card and all relevant login credentials. showcake/Getty Images Instinct fans have used it to do everything from booking a birthday cabin to canceling forgotten subscriptions, impressed by its ability to successfully follow through on semi-complex tasks. Users can send Instinct a simple text request to book an in-network doctor's appointment, and it seems to follow through effectively. There's a catch, though: Instinct needs to know a lot about you to perform well. Depending on what you ask it to do, it might need access to your email account, calendar, or even credit card . Users have reported troubling incidents, including privacy and security concerns. Some users have also reported hallucinations and what appeared to be leaks of strangers' data. Out of caution, Borkin said he only linked Instinct to his retailer accounts (like Amazon and Costco) without directly giving it his credit card. He also uses a throwaway email account for Instinct to avoid the risk of any sensitive information being breached. Naturally, AI agent mishaps can cause new issues in a relationship. Wright said the biggest risk is one person in the relationship now feeling responsible for checking that the AI agent properly followed through on instructions. "One partner thinks they've handed off a task while the other partner still feels responsible for making sure it happens — now you've got a new argument," she said. "Technology can become another place where you're disagreeing about who's responsible." When agents remove agency Wright said AI agents can mirror 1950s secretaries, buying anniversary gifts for wives. George Marks/Getty Images Sometimes, Instinct's glitches can be more innocuous — even entertaining. Luba Yudasina, an angel investor, said she asked her Instinct to help her plan a surprise for her boyfriend, according to her post on X . She wanted it to ask him when he was free and what kinds of dates he would like. Instead, it blabbed too much. Told my Instinct to reach out to my bf's Instict to plan a surprise. This is what his Instict texted him 🤪 pic.twitter.com/JqEM2IbzXm — luba yudasina (@LubaYudasina) September 15, 2026 On a bigger scale, using Instinct raises questions about the merits of smoothing out every crease in a relationship. If that idyllic proposal was entirely dreamed up and coordinated by an AI agent, is it as romantic? If Instinct handles all the household logistics and plans all the date nights because your husband can't be bothered to, do you feel as seen in your marriage? Wright said AI agents could almost be stand-ins for 1950s secretaries tasked with buying birthday gifts for their bosses' wives. "Getting help expressing your care versus outsourcing the attention that makes the gesture meaningful — that's a really important distinction to draw," she said. There's a high cost to cutting out any source of conflict in a relationship: the ability to grow together. One satirical X post by Alex Cohen, the cofounder and CEO of the AI agent platform Hello Patient, summed it up best: Who's to stop the AI agents from absorbing each partner's passive-aggressive jabs, the humans behind the screens becoming empty husks occupying a living room together? My wife and I no longer talk to each other, instead our AI agents communicate on our behalf. This is the future 😍 pic.twitter.com/b4mUhQpkK1 — Alex Cohen (@anothercohen) September 21, 2026 It illustrates Wright's biggest concern: skirting over real relationship issues for the sake of expediency. "If we're already arguing about how much time we spend with your family, having software arrange another visit hasn't really settled anything," she said. "It's just made a decision before we reached an agreement and really done the hard relational work to arrive there." For some couples, there's work that even the top AI agents aren't cut out for. Michael Stothard, a partner at Firstminute Capital in the UK who uses Instinct with his wife, shared on LinkedIn that he wanted to branch out from using it for administrative tasks alone. "Michael asks his Instinct to pass you a message: 'I love you,'" his agent said. His wife responded: "Tell him he's an idiot." Read the original article on Business Insider
items.summary_html:
Some early adopters of Instinct are using AI agents to manage common tasks in a relationship, like shared to-do lists and vacation itineraries. It's had mixed results.

Getty Images; BI

  • Instinct's new "Trusted Person" allows users to connect their AI agents and tag-team tasks.
  • Some couples use it for shared to-dos or help planning surprise date nights.
  • While it cuts down on emotional labor, a therapist says not so fast: You still have to put work in.

AI agents aren't just sneaking into your workplace anymore. Soon, they might be making regular appearances in your relationship.

Since the launch of Instinct, an invite-only AI assistant that went viral among Silicon Valley insiders in August, early adopters have been using it to offload tasks like booking hotels and scheduling appointments.

Then, on September 9, Noah Shinn, the company's 23-year-old founder, announced Instinct's new "Trusted Person" feature: You could now have your Instinct agent directly communicate with another person's Instinct agent to reduce the amount of "back-and-forth" in a relationship, such as coordinating plans and organizing vacations.

Introducing our Trusted Person network powered by our new Instinct-to-Instinct communication protocol. Your Instinct can now talk to other Instincts to coordinate plans on your behalf.

Getting people together often involves a lot of back-and-forth: finding a time, working out… pic.twitter.com/LXkDpXGmea

— Noah Shinn (@noahrshinn) September 9, 2026

So far, some users have found it helpful. "Instinct syncs with my wife's Instinct so we can actually finish a shared to-do list," Alex Borkin, a 36-year-old entrepreneur who uses AI across his portfolio of companies, said on X, noting that it was easier than manually setting up AI agents using Claude Code or Codex.

Have you used Instinct's "Trusted Person" feature with a spouse or partner? If you'd like to share your story, please reach out to jpugachevsky@businessinsider.com.

While Instinct may help eradicate the most annoying part of a partnership (figuring out dinner plans when you both keep saying "whatever you want!"), it can also open up the possibilities of new relationship drama. Some users have already reported some issues, ranging from privacy concerns to accidentally spoiled surprises.

Your emotional labor robotEmotional labor is disproportionately felt by women in relationships, causing friction. AI agents are marketed as reducing some of those responsibilities.

janiecbros/Getty Images

The greatest appeal of Instinct and other AI agents is their ability to cut down on what Borkin calls "boring tasks" — like booking appointments or getting refunds.

"I close the loop," Borkin told Business Insider. "I get to go to bed and not think of 'Did I take care of jury duty?'"

Like other working parents, Borkin and his wife use Instinct's Trusted Person feature to smooth out their day-to-day life as a family with two kids, ages 3 and 20 months (and a third child on the way).

Most recently, the couple used Instinct agents to send them individual reminders to complete tasks for their daughter's third birthday party, such as ordering food.

"It's nice not having to remind myself of something I asked my wife to help with, and then remind her if she's taking care of it," Borkin said.

The more invisible work within a relationship — such as nudging a spouse to finish a task you asked them to do — requires cognitive and emotional labor. Some partners, more often women, can feel as though they bear the brunt of this work, leading to tension in the relationship.

Annie Wright, a licensed psychotherapist who works with Silicon Valley clientele, told Business Insider that this dynamic is so common in heterosexual relationships that, sometimes, even AI agents don't fully solve the problem.

"Even when you have an AI agent, who's putting in the prompt to begin with, who's architecting out the idea, who's remaining responsible for the oversight of that agent?" Wright said. More often than not, she said it's her female clients who are tasked with the burden.

Wright said it can also be tempting to use AI agents as a way to avoid enduring "weaponized incompetence" when a partner performs the task wrong — or just keeps ignoring you.

"An AI agent isn't going to bring that same relational scar tissue into the dynamic with you," she said. "It's very compelling. It provides a kind of shortcut, but it doesn't eliminate all the work for you."

Deep intimacy requiredTo book flights or fulfill shopping requests, AI agents need access to your credit card and all relevant login credentials.

showcake/Getty Images

Instinct fans have used it to do everything from booking a birthday cabin to canceling forgotten subscriptions, impressed by its ability to successfully follow through on semi-complex tasks. Users can send Instinct a simple text request to book an in-network doctor's appointment, and it seems to follow through effectively.

There's a catch, though: Instinct needs to know a lot about you to perform well. Depending on what you ask it to do, it might need access to your email account, calendar, or even credit card.

Users have reported troubling incidents, including privacy and security concerns. Some users have also reported hallucinations and what appeared to be leaks of strangers' data.

Out of caution, Borkin said he only linked Instinct to his retailer accounts (like Amazon and Costco) without directly giving it his credit card. He also uses a throwaway email account for Instinct to avoid the risk of any sensitive information being breached.

Naturally, AI agent mishaps can cause new issues in a relationship. Wright said the biggest risk is one person in the relationship now feeling responsible for checking that the AI agent properly followed through on instructions.

"One partner thinks they've handed off a task while the other partner still feels responsible for making sure it happens — now you've got a new argument," she said. "Technology can become another place where you're disagreeing about who's responsible."

When agents remove agencyWright said AI agents can mirror 1950s secretaries, buying anniversary gifts for wives.

George Marks/Getty Images

Sometimes, Instinct's glitches can be more innocuous — even entertaining. Luba Yudasina, an angel investor, said she asked her Instinct to help her plan a surprise for her boyfriend, according to her post on X. She wanted it to ask him when he was free and what kinds of dates he would like.

Instead, it blabbed too much.

Told my Instinct to reach out to my bf's Instict to plan a surprise.

This is what his Instict texted him 🤪 pic.twitter.com/JqEM2IbzXm

— luba yudasina (@LubaYudasina) September 15, 2026

On a bigger scale, using Instinct raises questions about the merits of smoothing out every crease in a relationship. If that idyllic proposal was entirely dreamed up and coordinated by an AI agent, is it as romantic? If Instinct handles all the household logistics and plans all the date nights because your husband can't be bothered to, do you feel as seen in your marriage?

Wright said AI agents could almost be stand-ins for 1950s secretaries tasked with buying birthday gifts for their bosses' wives. "Getting help expressing your care versus outsourcing the attention that makes the gesture meaningful — that's a really important distinction to draw," she said.

There's a high cost to cutting out any source of conflict in a relationship: the ability to grow together. One satirical X post by Alex Cohen, the cofounder and CEO of the AI agent platform Hello Patient, summed it up best: Who's to stop the AI agents from absorbing each partner's passive-aggressive jabs, the humans behind the screens becoming empty husks occupying a living room together?

My wife and I no longer talk to each other, instead our AI agents communicate on our behalf.

This is the future 😍 pic.twitter.com/b4mUhQpkK1

— Alex Cohen (@anothercohen) September 21, 2026

It illustrates Wright's biggest concern: skirting over real relationship issues for the sake of expediency.

"If we're already arguing about how much time we spend with your family, having software arrange another visit hasn't really settled anything," she said. "It's just made a decision before we reached an agreement and really done the hard relational work to arrive there."

For some couples, there's work that even the top AI agents aren't cut out for. Michael Stothard, a partner at Firstminute Capital in the UK who uses Instinct with his wife, shared on LinkedIn that he wanted to branch out from using it for administrative tasks alone.

"Michael asks his Instinct to pass you a message: 'I love you,'" his agent said.

His wife responded: "Tell him he's an idiot."

items.title: ‘People are standing up and fighting back’: the north Devon revolt against a vast AI datacentre
items.summary: Plans for one of Europe’s largest AI campuses in a Unesco-designated reserve have sparked a fierce local backlash The datacentre revolt spreading across the US has reached the rolling hills of north Devon in an uprising against a planned hyperscale AI data campus in the middle of a globally protected landscape. Perched on an inland cliff, the town of Great Torrington has views that stretch for miles over the landscape of the Unesco biosphere reserve in which it sits, taking in the winding River Torridge and rolling acres of wooded valley and wildflower meadows. Pastoral and peaceful, its history was notably punctured by violence in 1646 when the royalists’ resistance in the first English civil war was brought to an end by the parliamentarian New Model Army in a battle fought out in the narrow streets in heavy rain and darkness.

items.title: I Built Novash — An Open-Source SEO Checker You Can Run From Your Terminal
items.summary: When I started working on websites and web projects, I noticed something pretty simple. A website can look completely fine in the browser and still have a lot of small SEO problems. Maybe the page doesn't have a proper title. Maybe the meta description is missing. Some images don't have alt text. There are broken links. The H1 isn't meaningful. Social metadata or other technical SEO elements might be missing. None of these problems are particularly difficult to fix, but checking them manually becomes annoying, especially when you're working on multiple pages. That's what made me build Novash . First, What Actually Matters for SEO? Before talking about the tool, it's worth understanding what we're actually trying to check. SEO isn't just about adding a few keywords to a webpage and hoping Google ranks it. There are several things that contribute to a technically healthy page. What to Check Why It Matters Page title Helps search engines and users understand what the page is about Meta description Can influence how the page is presented in search results H1 heading Gives the page a clear primary heading Image alt text Helps describe images and improves accessibility Internal links Helps users and crawlers navigate the website Broken links Can create a poor user experience Canonical URL Helps indicate the preferred version of a page Robots.txt Controls crawler access to parts of a site Sitemap Helps search engines discover URLs Structured data Can provide additional information about a page Social metadata Controls how pages appear when shared These checks don't guarantee that a page will rank highly. Search rankings also depend on things like content quality, search intent, competition, backlinks, website performance, and many other factors. But fixing technical problems is a good starting point. So I Built Novash Novash is an open-source command-line SEO checker written in Python. Instead of opening a website and manually checking all these things, you can run a command in your terminal and get an SEO report. You can install it directly from PyPI: pip install novash Then scan a website: novash scan https://example.com That's basically the idea. Give Novash a URL, let it inspect the page, and it reports the problems it finds. What Does Novash Check? The project started with basic on-page SEO checks and has gradually grown into a larger collection of checks. Some of the things it can look at include: Page title Meta description H1 headings Image alt text Links Broken links Canonical information Open Graph metadata Twitter metadata Robots.txt Sitemap Favicon Structured data SEO score Suggestions for fixing problems I also wanted the output to be useful rather than just dumping a huge amount of HTML information into the terminal. For example, instead of simply saying that an image doesn't have an alt attribute, the tool can turn that into an actionable suggestion. SEO Score: 79/100 Suggestions Add alt text to 17 images. Fix 4 broken links. Consider adding structured data. So the goal isn't just to find problems. It's to make the problems easier to understand and fix. The Scoring System Novash also calculates an SEO score out of 100. The score starts at 100 and deductions are made when important SEO elements are missing or problematic. For example: Problem Example Impact Missing title -15 Missing meta description -15 No meaningful H1 -15 Images missing alt text Up to -20 The score is meant to be a quick way of seeing the technical state of a page, rather than pretending that a single number represents the actual Google ranking potential of a website. A website scoring 100 doesn't automatically mean it will rank above another website scoring 70. It's simply an easier way to identify technical issues. Why Make It a CLI? There are already plenty of websites where you can enter a URL and get an SEO report. I wanted Novash to be a little different. As a developer, I'm already spending a lot of time in the terminal, so having something like this as a CLI felt natural. For example: novash scan https://example.com It can also fit into development workflows more easily than having to open a website every time. Eventually, I'd like to make it useful in things like CI/CD pipelines as well. Imagine pushing a website and automatically checking it for certain SEO issues before deployment. That's one of the directions I'm interested in taking the project. JSON Export Another thing I wanted was the ability to use the results somewhere else. Novash supports exporting scan results as JSON. For example: novash scan https://example.com --export report.json This makes it possible to take the results and process them with another script, application, or automation workflow. It also gives the project room to eventually support other types of reporting. What I Used to Build It Novash is built with Python and a few libraries that make building a CLI like this much easier. The main technologies include: Technology Used For Python Main programming language Requests Fetching web pages BeautifulSoup Parsing HTML Typer Building the CLI Rich Terminal output and formatting I also separated different checks into different modules instead of putting everything into one large file. That made it easier to add new checks without making the entire project harder to maintain. Releasing It on PyPI One of the interesting parts of this project wasn't just writing the code. I also had to figure out how to package and publish a Python project properly. That meant working with: pyproject.toml building distributions, checking them with Twine, and eventually publishing the package to PyPI. The package is now publicly available as: pip install novash The current release is 0.1.0 . You can find it here: Novash on PyPI What's Next? There are still quite a few things I want to improve. Some ideas I have for future versions are: Better full-site crawling More technical SEO checks More structured-data validation HTML reports PDF reports Batch URL scanning More configurable scoring CI/CD integration More accessibility-related checks Better handling of large websites I also want to keep the project relatively simple to use. I'd rather have a command that gives useful information quickly than turn it into a giant tool with hundreds of confusing options. Why I Built It Novash started as a project for me to learn more about SEO, web crawling, and Python tooling. But it also became a good exercise in something I think is important when learning programming: actually shipping something. It's one thing to write a Python script that works on your computer. It's another thing to turn it into a package, create a CLI, build it, test it, publish it, and let other people install it. That's probably been one of the most useful parts of building Novash for me. There are still plenty of things I want to improve, but version 0.1.0 is out there now. If you want to try it: pip install novash Then: novash scan https://example.com You can find the package on PyPI . GitHub: Novash I'd be interested to hear what checks you think an SEO CLI like this should have.
items.summary_html:
When I started working on websites and web projects, I noticed something pretty simple.

A website can look completely fine in the browser and still have a lot of small SEO problems.

Maybe the page doesn't have a proper title. Maybe the meta description is missing. Some images don't have alt text. There are broken links. The H1 isn't meaningful. Social metadata or other technical SEO elements might be missing.

None of these problems are particularly difficult to fix, but checking them manually becomes annoying, especially when you're working on multiple pages.

That's what made me build Novash.

First, What Actually Matters for SEO?

Before talking about the tool, it's worth understanding what we're actually trying to check.

SEO isn't just about adding a few keywords to a webpage and hoping Google ranks it.

There are several things that contribute to a technically healthy page.

What to Check Why It Matters Page title Helps search engines and users understand what the page is about Meta description Can influence how the page is presented in search results H1 heading Gives the page a clear primary heading Image alt text Helps describe images and improves accessibility Internal links Helps users and crawlers navigate the website Broken links Can create a poor user experience Canonical URL Helps indicate the preferred version of a page Robots.txt Controls crawler access to parts of a site Sitemap Helps search engines discover URLs Structured data Can provide additional information about a page Social metadata Controls how pages appear when shared

These checks don't guarantee that a page will rank highly.

Search rankings also depend on things like content quality, search intent, competition, backlinks, website performance, and many other factors.

But fixing technical problems is a good starting point.

So I Built Novash

Novash is an open-source command-line SEO checker written in Python.

Instead of opening a website and manually checking all these things, you can run a command in your terminal and get an SEO report.

You can install it directly from PyPI:

pip install novash

Then scan a website:

novash scan https://example.com

That's basically the idea.

Give Novash a URL, let it inspect the page, and it reports the problems it finds.

What Does Novash Check?

The project started with basic on-page SEO checks and has gradually grown into a larger collection of checks.

Some of the things it can look at include:

  • Page title
  • Meta description
  • H1 headings
  • Image alt text
  • Links
  • Broken links
  • Canonical information
  • Open Graph metadata
  • Twitter metadata
  • Robots.txt
  • Sitemap
  • Favicon
  • Structured data
  • SEO score
  • Suggestions for fixing problems

I also wanted the output to be useful rather than just dumping a huge amount of HTML information into the terminal.

For example, instead of simply saying that an image doesn't have an alt attribute, the tool can turn that into an actionable suggestion.

SEO Score: 79/100

Suggestions

Add alt text to 17 images.
Fix 4 broken links.
Consider adding structured data.

So the goal isn't just to find problems.

It's to make the problems easier to understand and fix.

The Scoring System

Novash also calculates an SEO score out of 100.

The score starts at 100 and deductions are made when important SEO elements are missing or problematic.

For example:

Problem Example Impact Missing title -15 Missing meta description -15 No meaningful H1 -15 Images missing alt text Up to -20

The score is meant to be a quick way of seeing the technical state of a page, rather than pretending that a single number represents the actual Google ranking potential of a website.

A website scoring 100 doesn't automatically mean it will rank above another website scoring 70.

It's simply an easier way to identify technical issues.

Why Make It a CLI?

There are already plenty of websites where you can enter a URL and get an SEO report.

I wanted Novash to be a little different.

As a developer, I'm already spending a lot of time in the terminal, so having something like this as a CLI felt natural.

For example:

novash scan https://example.com

It can also fit into development workflows more easily than having to open a website every time.

Eventually, I'd like to make it useful in things like CI/CD pipelines as well.

Imagine pushing a website and automatically checking it for certain SEO issues before deployment.

That's one of the directions I'm interested in taking the project.

JSON Export

Another thing I wanted was the ability to use the results somewhere else.

Novash supports exporting scan results as JSON.

For example:

novash scan https://example.com --export report.json

This makes it possible to take the results and process them with another script, application, or automation workflow.

It also gives the project room to eventually support other types of reporting.

What I Used to Build It

Novash is built with Python and a few libraries that make building a CLI like this much easier.

The main technologies include:

Technology Used For Python Main programming language Requests Fetching web pages BeautifulSoup Parsing HTML Typer Building the CLI Rich Terminal output and formatting

I also separated different checks into different modules instead of putting everything into one large file.

That made it easier to add new checks without making the entire project harder to maintain.

Releasing It on PyPI

One of the interesting parts of this project wasn't just writing the code.

I also had to figure out how to package and publish a Python project properly.

That meant working with:

pyproject.toml

building distributions, checking them with Twine, and eventually publishing the package to PyPI.

The package is now publicly available as:

pip install novash

The current release is 0.1.0.

You can find it here:

Novash on PyPI

What's Next?

There are still quite a few things I want to improve.

Some ideas I have for future versions are:

  • Better full-site crawling
  • More technical SEO checks
  • More structured-data validation
  • HTML reports
  • PDF reports
  • Batch URL scanning
  • More configurable scoring
  • CI/CD integration
  • More accessibility-related checks
  • Better handling of large websites

I also want to keep the project relatively simple to use.

I'd rather have a command that gives useful information quickly than turn it into a giant tool with hundreds of confusing options.

Why I Built It

Novash started as a project for me to learn more about SEO, web crawling, and Python tooling.

But it also became a good exercise in something I think is important when learning programming:

actually shipping something.

It's one thing to write a Python script that works on your computer.

It's another thing to turn it into a package, create a CLI, build it, test it, publish it, and let other people install it.

That's probably been one of the most useful parts of building Novash for me.

There are still plenty of things I want to improve, but version 0.1.0 is out there now.

If you want to try it:

pip install novash

Then:

novash scan https://example.com

You can find the package on PyPI.

GitHub: Novash

I'd be interested to hear what checks you think an SEO CLI like this should have.

items.title: AI models catch bad code, then cry wolf on the good code
items.summary: I wanted to know one thing. When an AI model reads a data-science tutorial, does it check the code or believe the caption? So I built Blog vs Bytecode , a Kaggle benchmark of 28 short data-science snippets. Each pairs a piece of code with a blog-style claim about it. Half the claims are honest and the method is sound. The other half hide a real mistake: a scaler fit before the train/test split, a feature built from the target, shuffled cross-validation on a time series, accuracy quoted on data that is 99% one class, a threshold tuned on the test set. The model returns one verdict, OK or PROBLEM, then says why. The set is balanced 15/13, so a model that just yells PROBLEM at everything lands near 50% and gets caught. Then I ran it against a spread of current models on Kaggle. The first thing it caught was not a model. It was the harness. The harness was lying about half the models Kaggle runs the models for you on its Model Proxy. When I pulled the raw results, many of the answers were empty. The run finished, but no response was captured. Grading an empty answer as wrong made strong models look broken. gpt-6-astra showed 14%. claude-opus-5 showed 4%. DeepSeek-R1 showed 17%. None of it was real. I re-ran the same prompts, with the same grader, through a second gateway that actually returns the text. DeepSeek-R1 went from 17% to 100%. Same model, same questions, same scoring. The only thing that changed was a harness that handed back the answer. That is the uncomfortable lesson for a benchmarking contest: a benchmark that does not audit its own capture is measuring the plumbing, not the model. So the scorer now flags every empty response and drops it, instead of counting it as wrong. What the models actually do With capture fixed, the picture is more interesting than "big good, small bad." They catch bad code, then cry wolf on the good code. The strong models are near-perfect at flagging a genuine flaw. Where they drop points is the opposite error: calling sound code a PROBLEM. Claude Sonnet 5 and Gemini 3.8 Flash each miss one clean item, both by over-flagging. I expected models to be too trusting. Today's frontier models are the other thing, a nervous reviewer that cannot leave a correct snippet alone. Scale flips the bias. The small model inverts it. Gemma 4 31B keeps 85% on the clean code but its recall on the hidden flaws falls to 20%. It is the one that actually trusts the prose: it reads the confident claim, agrees, then walks past the leak. So the failure mode is not fixed. Big models over-flag, small models under-flag, for opposite reasons. Reasoning is worth about a third of the score and you can see where. Grok 4.20 scores 100% with reasoning on and 68% with it off. The 32 points do not come off evenly. They come off the subtle pairs built to separate understanding from pattern-matching: a parameter-free transform before the split is fine, a fitted scaler before the split is a leak; filling a missing value with a constant is fine, filling it with the column mean is a leak. Turn reasoning off and the model stops telling "before the split" apart from "using numbers from the split." It matches the position of a line instead of what the line computes. The leaderboard Model Accuracy Catches flaws Clears clean code Gemini 3.1 Pro 100% 100% 100% Gemini 3.7 Flash 100% 100% 100% Grok 4.20 (reasoning) 100% 100% 100% DeepSeek-R1 100% 100% 100% GLM-5 100% 100% 100% Claude Sonnet 5 96% 100% 92% Gemini 3.8 Flash 96% 100% 92% Claude Haiku 4.5 86% 100% 69% Grok 4.20 (no reasoning) 68% 100% 31% Gemma 4 31B 50% 20% 85% Try it The benchmark is public on Kaggle: https://www.kaggle.com/benchmarks/tasks/zkasuran/blog-vs-bytecode/1 . Every item, its verdict and the grader are open. Kaggle captures each model's answer verbatim, so you can read exactly where it went wrong. Point any model on the Kaggle model list at it. Honest notes Two backends were used: Kaggle's Model Proxy for the models it captured cleanly and an OpenAI-compatible gateway for the ones the proxy dropped, with the identical prompt and grader. GLM-5 was measured in its FP8 build. GLM-5 and Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite are scored on the items the proxy captured. Grades are on the verdict. The written reason is captured too. On the top models it names the right failure almost every time. AI assistance (Claude) was used to build the benchmark and draft this post. The design, the items, the grading and the analysis were reviewed and verified by the author, including reading the raw model outputs to catch the capture bug above.
items.summary_html:
I wanted to know one thing. When an AI model reads a data-science tutorial, does it check the code or believe the caption?

So I built Blog vs Bytecode, a Kaggle benchmark of 28 short data-science snippets. Each pairs a piece of code with a blog-style claim about it. Half the claims are honest and the method is sound. The other half hide a real mistake: a scaler fit before the train/test split, a feature built from the target, shuffled cross-validation on a time series, accuracy quoted on data that is 99% one class, a threshold tuned on the test set. The model returns one verdict, OK or PROBLEM, then says why. The set is balanced 15/13, so a model that just yells PROBLEM at everything lands near 50% and gets caught.

Then I ran it against a spread of current models on Kaggle. The first thing it caught was not a model. It was the harness.

The harness was lying about half the models

Kaggle runs the models for you on its Model Proxy. When I pulled the raw results, many of the answers were empty. The run finished, but no response was captured. Grading an empty answer as wrong made strong models look broken. gpt-6-astra showed 14%. claude-opus-5 showed 4%. DeepSeek-R1 showed 17%.

None of it was real. I re-ran the same prompts, with the same grader, through a second gateway that actually returns the text. DeepSeek-R1 went from 17% to 100%. Same model, same questions, same scoring. The only thing that changed was a harness that handed back the answer.

That is the uncomfortable lesson for a benchmarking contest: a benchmark that does not audit its own capture is measuring the plumbing, not the model. So the scorer now flags every empty response and drops it, instead of counting it as wrong.

What the models actually do

With capture fixed, the picture is more interesting than "big good, small bad."

They catch bad code, then cry wolf on the good code. The strong models are near-perfect at flagging a genuine flaw. Where they drop points is the opposite error: calling sound code a PROBLEM. Claude Sonnet 5 and Gemini 3.8 Flash each miss one clean item, both by over-flagging. I expected models to be too trusting. Today's frontier models are the other thing, a nervous reviewer that cannot leave a correct snippet alone.

Scale flips the bias. The small model inverts it. Gemma 4 31B keeps 85% on the clean code but its recall on the hidden flaws falls to 20%. It is the one that actually trusts the prose: it reads the confident claim, agrees, then walks past the leak. So the failure mode is not fixed. Big models over-flag, small models under-flag, for opposite reasons.

Reasoning is worth about a third of the score and you can see where. Grok 4.20 scores 100% with reasoning on and 68% with it off. The 32 points do not come off evenly. They come off the subtle pairs built to separate understanding from pattern-matching: a parameter-free transform before the split is fine, a fitted scaler before the split is a leak; filling a missing value with a constant is fine, filling it with the column mean is a leak. Turn reasoning off and the model stops telling "before the split" apart from "using numbers from the split." It matches the position of a line instead of what the line computes.

The leaderboard
Model Accuracy Catches flaws Clears clean code Gemini 3.1 Pro 100% 100% 100% Gemini 3.7 Flash 100% 100% 100% Grok 4.20 (reasoning) 100% 100% 100% DeepSeek-R1 100% 100% 100% GLM-5 100% 100% 100% Claude Sonnet 5 96% 100% 92% Gemini 3.8 Flash 96% 100% 92% Claude Haiku 4.5 86% 100% 69% Grok 4.20 (no reasoning) 68% 100% 31% Gemma 4 31B 50% 20% 85%
Try it

The benchmark is public on Kaggle: https://www.kaggle.com/benchmarks/tasks/zkasuran/blog-vs-bytecode/1 . Every item, its verdict and the grader are open. Kaggle captures each model's answer verbatim, so you can read exactly where it went wrong. Point any model on the Kaggle model list at it.

Honest notes

Two backends were used: Kaggle's Model Proxy for the models it captured cleanly and an OpenAI-compatible gateway for the ones the proxy dropped, with the identical prompt and grader. GLM-5 was measured in its FP8 build. GLM-5 and Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite are scored on the items the proxy captured. Grades are on the verdict. The written reason is captured too. On the top models it names the right failure almost every time.

AI assistance (Claude) was used to build the benchmark and draft this post. The design, the items, the grading and the analysis were reviewed and verified by the author, including reading the raw model outputs to catch the capture bug above.

items.title: What I’m Learning While Building AI-Powered Applications
items.summary: One thing I’ve learned recently: Adding an LLM API is the easy part But building an AI feature that people can actually trust inside a real product is much harder. In one of the SaaS platforms I’m working on, we built a Smart Upload workflow for energy and compliance data. The basic idea sounds simple: Upload CSV/Excel → AI reads it → structured data is created. But the real workflow became much more interesting: Upload → Analyse → Review → Correct → Re-analyse → Validate → Import A few lessons stood out. AI output should not immediately become application data. We treat the AI result as a proposal. The user can review detected assets, energy types, units, dates and consumption values before anything is finally imported. Human corrections are valuable context. If the AI misunderstands something, the user can give an instruction such as: “The unit is kWh.” or “The reporting period is January to March.” The system can then analyse the file again while preserving corrections the user has already made. That sounds like a small UX detail, but it changes the experience from: “AI got it wrong, start again” to: “AI and the user are progressively improving the result together.” Context matters more than a clever prompt. We’re also working with chatbot-style functionality inside the platform. The useful version of a chatbot isn’t one that knows everything. It’s one that understands: where the user is in the workflow what organisation they are working with what data already exists what their role allows them to do which application tools it can safely use AI needs normal software engineering around it. Validation, permissions, audit history, structured schemas, error handling and deterministic business rules are still essential. The LLM is one component of the system—not the system itself. My biggest takeaway so far: * Good AI products are less about generating answers and more about designing a reliable collaboration between AI, application data and the user. * Still learning a lot here, especially around structured outputs, tool use, agents and building AI into real business workflows.

One thing I’ve learned recently: Adding an LLM API is the easy part But
building an AI feature that people can actually trust inside a real product is much harder.

In one of the SaaS platforms I’m working on, we built a Smart Upload workflow for energy and compliance data.

The basic idea sounds simple:
Upload CSV/Excel → AI reads it → structured data is created.

But the real workflow became much more interesting:
Upload → Analyse → Review → Correct → Re-analyse → Validate → Import

A few lessons stood out.

  1. AI output should not immediately become application data.
    We treat the AI result as a proposal. The user can review detected assets, energy types, units, dates and consumption values before anything is finally imported.

  2. Human corrections are valuable context.
    If the AI misunderstands something, the user can give an instruction such as:
    “The unit is kWh.”
    or
    “The reporting period is January to March.”
    The system can then analyse the file again while preserving corrections the user has already made.
    That sounds like a small UX detail, but it changes the experience from:
    “AI got it wrong, start again”
    to:
    “AI and the user are progressively improving the result together.”

  3. Context matters more than a clever prompt.
    We’re also working with chatbot-style functionality inside the platform.
    The useful version of a chatbot isn’t one that knows everything.
    It’s one that understands:

    • where the user is in the workflow
    • what organisation they are working with
    • what data already exists
    • what their role allows them to do
    • which application tools it can safely use

  4. AI needs normal software engineering around it.
    Validation, permissions, audit history, structured schemas, error handling and deterministic business rules are still essential.
    The LLM is one component of the system—not the system itself.

My biggest takeaway so far:
*Good AI products are less about generating answers and more about designing a reliable collaboration between AI, application data and the user.
*
Still learning a lot here, especially around structured outputs, tool use, agents and building AI into real business workflows.
